paragraphs.text: Lesson 3. Starting a new sport.
Joey is telling his brother, Brent, about the new sport he wants to try.
Listen to their conversation and do your best to answer the comprehension questions below.
I think I'm going to try out for the City Hockey Team this year.
You might want to think twice about that.
This isn't field hockey, it's ice hockey, and brawls are part of the game.
Those players eat guys like you for breakfast.
You're just as bad as mom.
I'm your older brother. It's my job to look out for you.
It's not like I'm joining the Army, it's just a local hockey league.
Joey, have you seen the size of the guys on those teams?
They eat, sleep, and breathe hockey.
If you step out onto the ice with them, they'll pulverize you.
They will not. Maybe small, but I'm fast.
Not a wimp. Last year I led the school's field hockey team to the National Championship.
I can handle it.
Oh really? Have you ever put on a pair of hockey skates?
Well, I go skating with Amy all the time. I'm sure there isn't much difference.
Hockey skates are different from the ones you wear when you take Amy out on a date.
And have you ever tried to dodge an angry player charging at you on ice skates?
Can't say I have. But how hard can it be? I mean I'm pretty agile and I got good reflexes.
No offense, Joey. But I've seen you skate and you're not exactly a pro.
So I'll practice. Maybe even take some private lessons to get up to speed.
I'm telling you, the high school hockey team is the best place for you to learn to skate
and learn the game.
They don't take it seriously though. The City League is the real deal. Sometimes scouts from the NHL
come and watch the games.
Right. And you're likely to have your butt firmly planted on the bench.
You'd be the least experienced guy on the team.
So what makes you think you'll even get any playing time?
Hmm, yeah. I guess it would suck to train and train and then watch most of the game from the sidelines.
Maybe the high school hockey team would be the best place for me to get a piece of the action.
Now you're using your head. Hey, the first thing we need to do is get you some real skates.
Let's head over to the rink and see if they have a pair of skates for sale in the shop.
Let's learn the vocabulary from Joey and Brent's conversation about starting a new sport.
Joey says, I think I'm going to try out for the City Hockey team.
This phrasal verb, try out for, means try to get on the team.
When you have a sports team that doesn't accept everybody, the players need to try out for the team.
They demonstrate their skills and abilities in the hopes of being selected for the team.
Brent says, you might want to think twice about that.
Think twice means reconsider.
Think again to make sure that you are not going to make a mistake.
Brent says, this isn't field hockey, it's ice hockey and brawls are part of the game.
Brawls are fights, usually referring to a physical fight, a fist fight between two or more people.
Brent also says, those players eat guys like you for breakfast.
Eat guys like you for breakfast is a slang way to say that the players are much tougher and stronger than you.
Brent says, it's his job to look out for Joey.
Look out for someone means to take care of that person's safety and best interests.
Joey says, it's not like I'm joining the army, it's just the local hockey league.
A league is a group of sports teams that compete against each other.
Brent emphasizes the size of the guys on the city hockey teams.
He tells Joey, if you step out onto the ice with them, they'll pulverize you.
Pulverize means break into small pieces.
Obviously Brent is exaggerating here, Joey will not literally be broken into small pieces,
but this is just another way to say that the other guys are much bigger, stronger and tougher than Joey.
And Joey will be at a distinct disadvantage.
Joey gives a counterpoint, he says, I may be small, but I'm fast, I'm not a wimp.
The word wimp is a slang word meaning a weak and fearful person.
It's an insult to call somebody a wimp.
Joey has been skating before, but Brent asks him, have you ever tried to dodge an angry player
charging at you on ice skates?
The word dodge is a verb meaning to move out of the way of something in motion.
And the verb charging means rushing forward in attack.
So Brent is asking Joey if he has ever tried to move out of the way of an angry player rushing
forward in attack. Joey hasn't done this, but he asks how hard can it be?
I mean I'm pretty agile and I've got good reflexes.
The word agile is an adjective meaning able to move quickly and easily.
And Joey has good reflexes, reflexes refers to your ability to react quickly.
But Brent responds, no offense Joey, I've seen you skate and you're not exactly a pro.
The phrase no offense means don't be offended by what I'm going to say.
The phrase you're not exactly a pro means you're not very good at it.
But Joey says he'll take some private lessons in order to get up to speed.
This expression get up to speed means learn to function at a normal or expected level,
to catch up to the ability or knowledge level of others.
Brent recommends that Joey try out for the high school hockey team instead.
But Joey really wants to play in the city league.
He says the city league is the real deal.
If you describe something as the real deal, you're saying that it's authentic or serious,
it's very good, or it lives up to expectations.
Joey also says sometimes scouts from the NHL come and watch the games.
First of all, the NHL is the National Hockey League.
Those are the professional hockey teams in the United States.
And scouts are people who recruit athletes for professional teams.
Scouts go to minor games and observe the players.
They identify the players with the most talent and then invite them to the professional teams.
But Brent points out that Joey is likely to have his butt firmly planted on the bench.
This expression on the bench means sitting with the reserve players
and not playing in the actual game.
Joey acknowledges that it would suck to train and train and then watch most of the game from the sidelines.
This phrase, it would suck, is slang, meaning it would be disappointing, terrible or unfortunate.
The expression it would suck is very informal and could be offensive.
Another way to say it is, it would stink.
So, Joey says it would suck to train and then watch most of the game from the sidelines.
The sidelines is the place outside where the game or action is.
Joey says maybe the high school hockey team would be the best place for me to get a piece of the action.
Get a piece of the action means participate in an activity.
Brent approves of this idea. He says, now you're using your head.
Using your head means thinking clearly and intelligently.
And Brent suggests buying Joey some ice skates.
He says, let's head over to the rink and see if they have a pair for sale in the shop.
The phrasal verb head over means go and the rink is the place where you can go ice skating.
It's called an ice rink or rink for short.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice
and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
